```{r discussion-setup, include=FALSE}
library(dplyr)

# Resolve the project root
.find_root <- function(start = getwd()) {
  path <- normalizePath(start, winslash = "/")
  while (!file.exists(file.path(path, "_quarto.yml"))) {
    parent <- normalizePath(dirname(path), winslash = "/")
    if (parent == path) stop("Could not find project root (_quarto.yml)")
    path <- parent
  }
  path
}
.root <- .find_root()
.p <- function(...) file.path(.root, ...)

rep   <- read.csv(.p("results/11_repeatability/repeatability_summary.csv"))
pred  <- read.csv(.p("results/12_predictability/predictability_summary.csv"))
clust <- read.csv(.p("results/14_individual_traits/behaviour_clusters.csv"))

# ── Format helpers ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fmt <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(round(x, digits), format = "f", digits = digits)

# Repeatability
r_val  <- function(v) fmt(rep$R_cow_mean[rep$variable == v])
r_ci   <- function(v) paste0("[", fmt(rep$R_cow_lower[rep$variable == v]), ", ",
                                   fmt(rep$R_cow_upper[rep$variable == v]), "]")

# CVi
cvi_val <- function(v) fmt(rep$CVi_mean[rep$variable == v])
cvi_ci  <- function(v) paste0("[", fmt(rep$CVi_lower[rep$variable == v]), ", ",
                                    fmt(rep$CVi_upper[rep$variable == v]), "]")

# CVP
cvp_val <- function(v) fmt(pred$CVP_mean[pred$variable == v])
cvp_ci  <- function(v) paste0("[", fmt(pred$CVP_lower[pred$variable == v]), ", ",
                                    fmt(pred$CVP_upper[pred$variable == v]), "]")

# Derived summaries
r_min_var  <- rep$variable[which.min(rep$R_cow_mean)]
r_min_val  <- fmt(min(rep$R_cow_mean))
r_max_var  <- rep$variable[which.max(rep$R_cow_mean)]
r_max_val  <- fmt(max(rep$R_cow_mean))

cvp_min_val <- fmt(min(pred$CVP_mean))
cvp_max_val <- fmt(max(pred$CVP_mean))

cvi_max_var <- rep$variable[which.max(rep$CVi_mean)]
cvi_max_val <- fmt(max(rep$CVi_mean))

c1_vars <- clust$variable[clust$cluster == 1]
n_c1    <- length(c1_vars)

var_labels <- c(
  "feed_intake"                    = "daily feed intake",
  "feed_duration"                  = "daily feeding duration",
  "feed_visits"                    = "daily feeding visits",
  "water_intake"                   = "daily water intake",
  "water_duration"                 = "daily drinking duration",
  "water_visits"                   = "daily drinking visits",
  "total_actor"                    = "daily actor events",
  "total_reactor"                  = "daily reactor events",
  "number_of_non_nutritive_visits" = "daily non-nutritive visits",
  "median_pct_feed_remaining"      = "median proportion of feed remaining at visit start",
  "total_meals"                    = "daily meals",
  "median_meal_duration"           = "median meal duration",
  "median_visit_per_meal"          = "median visits per meal",
  "median_intake_per_meal"         = "median feed intake per meal",
  "median_feeding_pct_per_meal"    = "median percentage of meal time spent feeding",
  "median_non_nutritive_per_meal"  = "median non-nutritive visits per meal"
)

clean_label <- function(v) {
  labels <- var_labels[v]
  ifelse(is.na(labels), gsub("_", " ", v), unname(labels))
}
```

# 4. Discussion

This study illustrates how the use of existing data streams from electronic feeders and drinkers can be used to describe far richer behavioral information than is typically extracted. By developing the `moo4feed` R package, we introduced a standardized and reproducible pipeline for processing raw electronic feeder and drinker data and extracting behavioral variables that go beyond basic daily intake and visit counts. Using 16 variables spanning feeding, drinking, meal patterns, non-nutritive behavior, and social competition, we quantified repeatability and predictability for each variable, identified behaviors most informative for individual profiling, and used those behaviors to characterize four distinct cow types within the herd.

## 4.1 Repeatability and Predictability in Context

Our repeatability values ranged from `r r_min_val` to `r r_max_val`, with most variables falling between 0.38 and 0.64. This places the majority of our behavioral variables above the average repeatability value of R = 0.37 reported in a meta-analysis of 759 estimates across 114 studies and 98 species [@Bell2009], indicating that the behaviors captured from electronic feeders and drinkers likely reflect stable individual differences.

Two methodological points are worth noting when comparing our results to previous cattle work. First, none of the previous studies [@thomas2024; @carslake2022b; @occhiuto2022] reported CVi, the coefficient of individual variation. As articulated by Hertel et al. [-@hertel2020], CVi is essential for comparing the magnitude of among-individual differences across studies and populations because R is confounded by within-individual variance: a high R can result from either large among-individual differences or very low day-to-day variability within individuals. Without CVi, it is not possible to determine whether differences in R between studies reflect genuine differences in among-individual variation or merely differences in residual noise. Our study is the first in the cattle repeatability literature to report CVi alongside R, and we encourage future work to report both metrics to enable meaningful cross-study comparisons. Second, the comparison between our adult cow results and the calf results of Carslake et al. [-@carslake2022b] and Occhiuto et al. [-@occhiuto2022] should be interpreted cautiously. Bell et al. [-@Bell2009] noted that whether juveniles are more or less repeatable than adults of the same species remains an unanswered biological question with no clear directional prediction: juveniles may be less repeatable because they are undergoing rapid developmental change, or more repeatable because the costs of deviating from a developmental trajectory are high. Neave et al. [-@neave2020long] found that bold and exploratory traits were consistent within each rearing period (before and after weaning; after puberty to first lactation), but were not consistent across the pubertal transition, suggesting that major physiological changes at sexual maturation can disrupt previously stable behavioral profiles. The few within-species comparisons available show no consistent pattern. We therefore focus our direct comparisons on Thomas et al. [-@thomas2024], the only other study conducted in adult dairy cows.

For the variables directly comparable to Thomas et al. [-@thomas2024], our estimates are similar or higher. Our R for daily feeding duration (`r r_val("feed_duration")` `r r_ci("feed_duration")`) exceeds their R = 0.38 [0.35, 0.40] for daily feeding time in 2584 adult cows across 46 herds. This difference likely reflects methodological differences rather than a true biological divergence: Thomas et al. used neck-mounted sensors and aggregated data across diverse commercial herds; whereas our study used automated feeders with strict data filtering, removing days affected by illness, lameness, estrus, and other disruptions. These design choices reduce within-individual noise and would be expected to yield higher repeatability. 

Many of our highest-R variables capture behaviors that have never before been assessed for repeatability, which prevents comparison. Even our lowest R value (`r r_min_val`) is likely still biologically meaningful. Bell et al. [-@Bell2009] showed that many well-established personality traits in wild populations have R values between 0.20 and 0.40. For behaviors measured in the broader cattle literature but not in our study (e.g., lying bouts, space use), prior work reports R values ranging from 0.03 to 0.80 in calves and 0.21 to 0.38 in adult cows [@thomas2024; @carslake2022b; @occhiuto2022]. 

For predictability, our CVP values ranged from `r cvp_min_val` to `r cvp_max_val` across all 16 variables. This is notably lower than the cross-species mean CVP of 0.27 [0.22, 0.33] reported across 64 estimates from 39 datasets in a meta-analysis of behavioral and physiological traits [@mitchell2020]. For dairy calves, CVP values in the literature ranged from 0.13 [0.06, 0.21] (total meals; @carslake2022b) to 0.49 [0.35, 0.62] (core area used; @occhiuto2022). For adult dairy cows, Thomas et al. [-@thomas2024] reported CVP values ranging from 0.19 [0.18, 0.20] (daily feeding time) to 0.46 [0.44, 0.48] (mean lying bout duration), with higher values coming from bout-level metrics that are inherently more relabile than daily aggregates. Our corresponding CVP for daily feeding duration was `r cvp_val("feed_duration")` `r cvp_ci("feed_duration")`, which is close to Thomas et al.'s daily feeding time estimate and confirms that our daily-level metrics fall at the lower end of the adult cow range.

The uniformly low CVP values in our study likely reflect the strict data filtering that inflated our R estimates relative to previous work: by removing days disrupted by illness, lameness, estrus, and regrouping, we restricted our analyses to a stable baseline. This is a practically useful finding in its own right: under clean baseline conditions, CVP values were consistently low across all variables, and the variation in predictability across cows was modest. Whether individual cow types (e.g., the "fragmented feeders" identified in Section 3.3) show systematically higher within-individual variability during periods of health challenge, or whether predictability is better understood as a property of physiological state than of personality, is an important question for future work.

## 4.2 Novel Behavioral Variables

A key contribution of this study is showing that electronic feeders capture information well beyond what is typically reported. Standard analyses focus on daily feed and water intake, visit counts, and duration. By applying the `moo4feed` pipeline, we additionally derived variables capturing non-nutritive visits, social competition (actor and reactor replacement events), feeding efficiency (median percentage of meal time spent actively eating), feed access disadvantage (proportion of feed remaining at visit start), and meal fragmentation (median visits per meal). These variables have rarely been considered in the repeatability and predictability literature, which has focused primarily on daily aggregates of feeding and lying behaviors [@thomas2024; @carslake2022b; @occhiuto2022].

Among all variables, non-nutritive visits showed the largest CVi, with cows differ from one another by more than half the population mean in how often they visit feed bins without eating. Daily actor events and daily reactor events also showed high among-individual variation. In contrast, daily feed intake showed the smallest relative variation. The finding that cows are nearly indistinguishable from one another in daily feed intake, despite exhibiting different feeding profiles, suggests compensatory feeding: cows converge to similar intakes through different behavioral pathways. Cow 7068 (frequently replaced, but efficient and sustained feeder) and cow 5042 (fragmented, restless, but fast eater) both achieved high daily feed intakes through opposite strategies. This echoes Thomas et al. [-@thomas2024], who found high repeatability for total daily feeding time and interpreted it as cows compensating disrupted bouts by adjusting other feeding behaviors.

## 4.3 Behavioral Profiles and Cow Types

Personality has been defined as consistent differences in how individual animals respond across contexts and over time [@reale2007]. The four cow types we identified are grounded in variables that showed consistent and large among-individual variation, meaning these cows differed from one another in stable, characteristic ways throughout the study. However, we do not claim that this constitutes personality. Such assessment requires data capturing a more diverse range of variables spanning a longer time window, more diverse contexts, and ideally replication across farms and management systems. Nevertheless, the patterns we observed are consistent with the personality framework as behavioral differences were not explained purely by the fixed effects in our models. These sensor-derived behavioral profiles appear to reflect some aspects of personality or personality-like traits. It is worth noting that cows in this study were overstocked at the feeder (48 cows for 30 feed bins), which likely increased competition for feed access [@sheng2024redefining]. The profiles we identified may only be relevant under high-competition conditions [@schwanke2025graduate]. It is also important to note that although k-means assigns each cow to a single cluster, this is a hard partition imposed on what is in reality continuous variation. Cows near a cluster boundary share features of both adjacent types, and each profile describes a group's central tendency rather than a rigid category that every cow matches exactly.

The contrast between “contest-winning” and “frequently replaced” cows captures differences in competitive success at the feeder, not necessarily dominance. As we noted in previous work [@sheng2024redefining], replacement events should not be considered a clear proxy for dominance as these are likely associated with motivation to access fresh feed in intensive and competitive environment, in addition to social rank. What the cluster analysis captures is not who dominates whom, but who consistently initiates replacements and who consistently yields. The ‘contest-winning’ cluster thus likely includes cows with strong motivation to access fresh feed. Interestingly, some “frequently replaced” cows compensated for this disadvantage through sustained, efficient feeding during the time they did occupy a bin, while “contest-winning” cows, facing fewer disruptions, engaged in less non-nutritive behavior.

The "frequent drinker visitors" cluster stands out because these cows spent considerably more time at and returning to the drinkers without drinking more water, suggesting the behavior is not primarily driven by thirst. Cow 7150, whose case we highlighted, showed long drinking durations and frequent drinker visits during a period when THI remained consistently below 68, suggesting that this behavior was not related to heat load [@McDonald2020]. One speculative explanation is that these excessive drinker visits may resemble schedule-induced polydipsia, a phenomenon documented in rodents experiencing constrained and intermittent food access, where excessive drinking develops as a stereotypic behaviour unrelated to hydration [@falk1961; @mason1991stereotypies]. We do not have data to test this hypothesis directly, but we encourage future work to investigate whether a similar mechanism may exist in dairy cattle. 

## 4.4 Limitations

Several limitations warrant acknowledgment. Data were collected at a single research farm using Holstein dairy cows under specific management conditions, which limits direct generalizability to commercial herds with different pen designs, stocking densities, or feeding management. The dynamic group composition (approximately 6 cows entering and leaving the pen every 16 days) introduced ongoing social instability. 

A methodological strength of our study relative to previous work is the explicit assessment of variable distributions before model fitting. We examined each variable's distribution and selected Gaussian or lognormal likelihoods accordingly (Section 2.4). The choice of likelihood family matters because it affects the scale on which variance components are estimated and therefore the resulting R and CVi values.

For the total meals variable, we used a lognormal model (log transformation) because the raw distribution was strongly right-skewed. Although total meals is technically a count and could in principle be modeled with a negative binomial distribution, we chose the lognormal approach for two reasons. First, the primary goal was to compare repeatability and predictability across all 16 variables on a common scale. Using a different distributional family for one variable would have required simulation-based methods to extract comparable R and CVi estimates, making direct comparison across variables much more complex. Second, the same issue applies to feeding rate and drinking rate, which we excluded from the current analysis entirely because their distributions could not be adequately normalized even after log transformation. Fitting these variables with appropriate non-Gaussian families and deriving comparable repeatability metrics through simulation is beyond the scope of this paper but represents a worthwhile extension for future work.

## 4.5 Future Directions

Several new directions could be explored based on this work. First, the `moo4feed` R package should be applied to other species and study systems (e.g., goats, common waxbills) to evaluate whether the behavioral extraction pipeline and the analytical framework is generalizable beyond dairy cattle. The package was designed with flexibility in mind, and testing its applicability across diverse farm settings would strengthen its utility as a general tool for behavioral phenotyping.

Second, future research should explore the temporal and spatial dimensions of feeding behavior. Our analyses characterized what cows do on average across the day, but not when or where they choose to compete for access to food and water. An important yet unexplored dimension is circadian rhythms in competitive and feeding behaviors. @sheng2024redefining showed that more replacements happened during afternoon feed delivery compared to the morning feed delivery. Future work should examine whether individual cows differ in their circadian patterns of feeding and competition, and whether these patterns remain consistent across days. 

In addition, we observed that certain ‘popular’ bins attracted disproportionately high competition, even though fresh feed was delivered to all bins. These bins were the first few bins to receive fresh feed delivery, and they were closest to the entry pathway used by cows returning from milking. Cows likely differ in their temporal strategies: some may head straight to the most popular bins during peak competition times (arguably a risky, costly approach), while others may access fresh feed at the same high-competition time but choose less popular bins that still have fresh feed yet are more isolated from herd traffic. Understanding whether individual cows consistently adopt one temporal strategy over another would add a new dimension to behavioral profiling.

Third, future work should investigate social relationships between specific cows. Are there stable bonds within the herd, pairs that always feed together or next to each other? Are there strong antagonisms where particular individuals always replace each other? Understanding these dyadic patterns could enhance our understanding about the social network structure of farm animals.

Fourth, changes in these behaviors over time, and especially changes in a cow's predictability (a highly consistent cow suddenly showing large variation in her behavior), could serve as early indicators of disease or distress. The personality-dependent sickness behavior documented by Setser et al. [-@setser2024a] in calves, where fearful and active calves changed their lying behavior in opposite directions when sick, suggests that the four cow types identified here may respond to illness differently. Prospective validation of whether individual behavioral profiles predict the nature, direction, and timing of health-related behavioral changes would be the critical translational step toward individualized health monitoring. The individual cow narratives presented in Section 3.3 demosntrates the potential for continuous sensor-derived behavioral profiling and individualized monitoring, where significant departures from an established baseline could trigger producer alerts for veterinary follow-up.

Finally, while the `moo4feed` package currently takes in data from electronic feeders and drinkers, it was designed in a modular and flexible way. If computer vision systems or other technologies become available that can record which cow eats where and when, the package can accommodate these alternative data sources as long as they output the same fundamental information: individual identity, location, timing, and intake. Several of the most informative variables identified here (e.g., drinking duration, drinking visits, and feeding visit frequency) are in principle detectable from video-based monitoring systems that track animal identity and movement without specialised intake hardware, offering a path for farms that cannot justify the cost of electronic feeders. Even without any automated sensing, the four cow types described here provide a practical framework for farmers to note which cows often linger at the drinker or repeatedly switch bins without eating. These observations can be used to build an informal cow-specific baseline, making future departures from that norm (which may signal health changes) more readily detectable.
